::: {.solutions}

This is not a past paper — it is a **clinic**, built from the four graph questions you missed on the
Tyler mocks. Graphs was the pattern across every wrong answer, so the point here is not to see new
questions but to see *these* ones done properly, and to name the one skill each was testing.

Graphs is not a single skill. The four questions below hit three different ones, and it helps to know
which is which:

| Skill | Question | What it asks |
|---|---|---|
| **Read a graph, then use it** | Q1 (was Q18), Q2 (was Q9) | the graph is given; pull a fact off it and feed it in |
| **Sketch an unfamiliar relation** | Q3 (was Q20) | you produce the graph from an equation |
| **Solve by drawing** | Q4 (was Q19) | draw one curve, count where it meets a line |

Work them in order — the reading questions first, then the producing ones. Each closes with **where the
wrong options come from**, because on every one of these you chose a distractor, and the distractor tells
us exactly which step slipped.

## Question 1

::: {.question}
The diagram shows the graph of $y = f(x)$. The function $f$ attains its maximum value at $(0,3)$ and
$f(x) > 0$ for all values of $x$.

Find the difference between the maximum and minimum values of $\bigl(f(x)\bigr)^3 - 3f(x)$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $0$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **B** $4$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **C** $12$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **D** $18$ &nbsp;&nbsp;
**E** $20$

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "The given diagram: y = f(x) — maximum value 3 at (0,3), positive everywhere, tailing to 0."
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
x = np.linspace(-6, 6, 400); f = 3*np.exp(-x**2/4)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.0, 3.0))
ax.plot(x, f, color='#1f77b4', lw=2)
ax.plot(0, 3, 'o', color='#d62728')
ax.annotate('(0, 3)', (0, 3), (0.4, 3.05), fontsize=10, color='#d62728')
ax.axhline(0, color='0.6', lw=0.8); ax.axvline(0, color='0.6', lw=0.8)
ax.set_ylim(-0.5, 3.6); ax.set_xlabel('x'); ax.set_ylabel('y')
ax.set_title('y = f(x)', fontsize=11)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```
:::

The trap is to start differentiating $\bigl(f(x)\bigr)^3 - 3f(x)$ in $x$ — you cannot, you do not know
$f$. The move is a **substitution**: [let $w = f(x)$ and read the range of $w$ off the graph]{.hl}.
Because the graph tops out at $3$ and stays positive, $w$ runs over $0 < w \le 3$. Now the whole thing is
just the cubic $w^3 - 3w$ on that interval, and [you are back to a standard "turning points on a closed
interval" question]{.hl}.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(Set C/D Q18)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — function of a function; read the range off a graph, then treat it as a cubic on an interval
:::


**Substitute.** Let $w = f(x)$. From the graph, $f$ has a maximum value of $3$ (at $x=0$) and is always
positive, tailing towards $0$ far out. So as $x$ ranges over all reals, [$w$ takes every value in the
range]{.hl} $0 < w \le 3$.

The expression becomes $g(w) = w^3 - 3w$, and we want its maximum minus its minimum **for $w$ in
$(0,3]$**.

**Turning points.** Differentiate in $w$:
$$g'(w) = 3w^2 - 3 = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad w = 1 \ \ (\text{the } w=-1 \text{ root is outside } (0,3]).$$
So $g(1) = 1 - 3 = -2$ — a minimum, since $g''(w)=6w>0$ there.

**Check the ends of the interval** — a maximum on a closed interval can sit at an endpoint, not a turning
point:
$$g(w)\to 0 \ \text{ as } w\to 0^{+}, \qquad g(3) = 27 - 9 = 18.$$

So on $(0,3]$ the curve dips to a minimum of $-2$ at $w=1$, then climbs to $18$ at the right-hand end
$w=3$. The maximum is $18$, the minimum is $-2$, and the difference is
$$18 - (-2) = 20,$$
which is **option E**. $\blacksquare$

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "g(w)=w³−3w on the interval w ∈ (0,3]: minimum −2 at the turning point w=1, maximum 18 at the right endpoint w=3, so the difference is 20."
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

CURVE = '#1f77b4'; MARK = '#d62728'; ACCENT = '#2ca02c'

w = np.linspace(0, 3, 400)
g = w**3 - 3*w
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.2, 3.8))
ax.plot(w, g, color=CURVE, lw=2)
ax.plot(1, -2, 'o', color=MARK)
ax.annotate(r'min $(1,-2)$', (1, -2), (1.05, -4.5), fontsize=10, color=MARK)
ax.plot(3, 18, 'o', color=ACCENT)
ax.annotate(r'max $(3,18)$', (3, 18), (1.7, 15), fontsize=10, color=ACCENT)
ax.axhline(0, color='0.6', lw=0.8)
ax.set_title(r'$g(w)=w^3-3w$ on $(0,3]$:  $18-(-2)=20$', fontsize=11)
ax.set_xlabel('w'); ax.set_ylabel('g(w)'); ax.set_xlim(0, 3.1)

plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

**Where the wrong options come from.**

| | |
|---|---|
| **D** $18$ | Found the maximum $g(3)=18$ but took the minimum as $0$ (the $w\to0$ end) instead of the turning-point value $-2$. The turning point was missed. |
| **C** $12$ | Used the wrong range for $w$, e.g. $[0,\,\text{something}]$, or read the max at $w=2$. |
| **B** $4$ | Difference between the two turning-point values $g(\pm1)=\mp2$, i.e. $2-(-2)$ — forgot that $w$ cannot be negative here. |
| **A** $0$ | Assumed the expression is constant, or cancelled $w^3-3w$ incorrectly. |
:::

## Question 2

::: {.question}
The function $f(x)$ is such that $f(0)=0$ and $xf(x)<0$ for $x\neq0$. You are given that
$$\int_{-5}^{5} f(x)\,\mathrm dx = 2 \qquad\text{and}\qquad \int_{-5}^{5} \lvert f(x)\rvert\,\mathrm dx = 16.$$
Find
$$\int_{-5}^{5} f(\lvert x\rvert)\,\mathrm dx.$$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $-14$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **B** $-4$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **C** $0$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **D** $4$ &nbsp;&nbsp;
**E** $14$
:::

Two conditions decode the shape before you touch an integral. $xf(x)<0$ means [$f$ and $x$ always have
opposite signs]{.hl}: $f$ is **positive on the left** ($x<0$) and **negative on the right** ($x>0$). So
the two given integrals are a signed area and an unsigned area — call the left lump $A$ and the right lump
$B$. The real insight is the last one: [$f(\lvert x\rvert)$ is an even function]{.hl}, so its integral is
just twice the right-hand half.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(Set C/D Q9)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — symmetry and signed area; why $f(\lvert x\rvert)$ is an even function
:::


**Name the two areas.** Let $A$ be the (positive) area between the curve and the axis on $[-5,0]$, and
$B$ the area on $[0,5]$. Because $f>0$ on the left and $f<0$ on the right,
$$\int_{-5}^{0} f = +A, \qquad \int_{0}^{5} f = -B.$$

The two given facts become a pair of simultaneous equations:
$$\underbrace{A - B = 2}_{\int f = 2}, \qquad \underbrace{A + B = 16}_{\int |f| = 16}
\;\Longrightarrow\; A = 9,\ \ B = 7.$$

**Now the key step.** Let $g(x) = f(\lvert x\rvert)$. For any $x$, $g(-x) = f(\lvert -x\rvert) =
f(\lvert x\rvert) = g(x)$, so [$g$ is even — symmetric about the $y$-axis]{.hl}. An even function's
integral over a symmetric interval is twice one half:
$$\int_{-5}^{5} f(\lvert x\rvert)\,\mathrm dx = 2\int_{0}^{5} f(\lvert x\rvert)\,\mathrm dx
= 2\int_{0}^{5} f(x)\,\mathrm dx,$$
because on $[0,5]$ we have $\lvert x\rvert = x$. That last integral is $-B = -7$, so the answer is
$$2\times(-7) = -14,$$
which is **option A**. $\blacksquare$

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Top: the given f — positive lump A on the left, negative lump B on the right, with A−B=2 and A+B=16. Bottom: f(|x|) reflects the right-hand piece into the left, giving an even function whose integral is 2×(−B)=−14."
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

POS = '#2ca02c'; NEG = '#d62728'; CURVE = '#1f77b4'

fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(5.2, 8.0))

x = np.linspace(-5, 5, 400)
# an odd-ish f: positive for x<0, negative for x>0, f(0)=0
f = -np.sign(x)*np.abs(x)*np.exp(-np.abs(x)/3)*2.2

# --- top: f(x) ---
ax[0].plot(x, f, color=CURVE, lw=2)
ax[0].fill_between(x, f, 0, where=(x<0), color=POS, alpha=0.3)
ax[0].fill_between(x, f, 0, where=(x>0), color=NEG, alpha=0.3)
ax[0].axhline(0, color='0.5', lw=0.8); ax[0].axvline(0, color='0.5', lw=0.8)
ax[0].text(-3.2, 1.1, 'A = 9', color=POS, fontsize=12)
ax[0].text(2.2, -1.2, 'B = 7', color=NEG, fontsize=12)
ax[0].set_title(r'$y=f(x)$:  $A-B=2$, $A+B=16$', fontsize=11)
ax[0].set_xlabel('x'); ax[0].set_ylabel('f(x)')

# --- bottom: f(|x|) — even, both halves are the right-hand piece ---
g = -np.sign(np.abs(x))*np.abs(x)*np.exp(-np.abs(x)/3)*2.2  # = f(|x|): negative both sides
ax[1].plot(x, g, color=CURVE, lw=2)
ax[1].fill_between(x, g, 0, color=NEG, alpha=0.3)
ax[1].axhline(0, color='0.5', lw=0.8); ax[1].axvline(0, color='0.5', lw=0.8)
ax[1].text(-3.6, -1.2, '−B = −7', color=NEG, fontsize=11)
ax[1].text(2.2, -1.2, '−B = −7', color=NEG, fontsize=11)
ax[1].set_title(r'$y=f(|x|)$: even  $\Rightarrow$  $2\times(-7)=-14$', fontsize=11)
ax[1].set_xlabel('x'); ax[1].set_ylabel('f(|x|)')

plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

**Where the wrong options come from.**

| | |
|---|---|
| **E** $+14$ | The right idea ($2\int_0^5 f$) but the **wrong sign** — took the right-hand lump as $+7$, forgetting $f<0$ on $[0,5]$. |
| **D** $+4$ | Doubled the *given* integral: $2\times 2 = 4$. But $\int f(\lvert x\rvert) \ne 2\int f(x)$ — the left half changes. |
| **B** $-4$ | Right magnitude idea, wrong pairing of $A$ and $B$. |
| **C** $0$ | Assumed $f(\lvert x\rvert)$ is odd (so the integral vanishes) — it is **even**, the whole point of the question. |
:::

## Question 3

::: {.question}
Which of the following sketches shows the graph of
$$\sin\!\left(\frac{y}{x}\right) = \frac12 \qquad\text{for } -3\pi x \le y \le 3\pi x\,?$$
(The options are sketches A–F; several show sets of straight lines through the origin, one shows a wave.)
:::

The instinct is to picture a wave, because there is a $\sin$ in it — that is the trap, and it is why the
wavy options are there. But $\sin$ is applied to $\tfrac{y}{x}$, not to $x$, so [treat $\tfrac{y}{x}$ as a
single quantity]{.hl}. Solving $\sin(\text{that}) = \tfrac12$ forces $\tfrac{y}{x}$ to equal one of a
list of **constants**, and $\tfrac{y}{x} = \text{constant}$ is a **straight line through the origin**. So
the graph is [a fan of straight lines through the origin]{.hl}, not a curve.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(Set C/D Q20)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — sketching an implicit relation; recognising a family of straight lines through the origin
:::


**Let $u = \dfrac{y}{x}$.** The equation is $\sin u = \tfrac12$, whose solutions are
$$u = \frac{\pi}{6} + 2\pi k \qquad\text{or}\qquad u = \frac{5\pi}{6} + 2\pi k, \quad k\in\mathbb Z.$$

Each such $u$ is a fixed number, and $\dfrac{y}{x} = u$ means $y = ux$ — [a straight line through the
origin with gradient $u$]{.hl}. So the graph is a set of straight lines, one for each allowed $u$.

**Which lines survive the restriction?** The condition $-3\pi x \le y \le 3\pi x$ says
$-3\pi \le \dfrac{y}{x} \le 3\pi$ (and, since it needs $-3\pi x \le 3\pi x$, it holds only for
$x>0$ — the lines live in the right-hand half only). So keep the values of $u$ with
$\lvert u\rvert \le 3\pi \approx 9.4$:

$$u = \frac{\pi}{6},\ \frac{5\pi}{6},\ \frac{13\pi}{6},\ \frac{17\pi}{6}
\quad(\text{four with positive gradient}), \qquad
u = -\frac{7\pi}{6},\ -\frac{11\pi}{6}\quad(\text{two with negative gradient}).$$

That is **six straight lines through the origin, drawn only for $x>0$** — the sketch showing exactly that
fan of half-lines is **option B**. $\blacksquare$

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "The graph of sin(y/x)=½ on −3πx ≤ y ≤ 3πx: six straight half-lines through the origin (gradients π/6, 5π/6, 13π/6, 17π/6 and −7π/6, −11π/6), drawn only for x>0. Not a wave."
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

LINE = '#1f77b4'; EDGE = '#d62728'

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.2, 5.0))

gradients = [np.pi/6, 5*np.pi/6, 13*np.pi/6, 17*np.pi/6, -7*np.pi/6, -11*np.pi/6]
xs = np.linspace(0, 1.4, 10)
for m in gradients:
    ax.plot(xs, m*xs, color=LINE, lw=1.8)

# the bounding wedge y = ±3πx (x>0)
ax.plot(xs, 3*np.pi*xs, '--', color=EDGE, lw=1)
ax.plot(xs, -3*np.pi*xs, '--', color=EDGE, lw=1)
ax.text(1.42, 3*np.pi*1.42, r'$y=3\pi x$', color=EDGE, fontsize=9, va='center')
ax.text(1.42, -3*np.pi*1.42, r'$y=-3\pi x$', color=EDGE, fontsize=9, va='center')

ax.axhline(0, color='0.6', lw=0.8); ax.axvline(0, color='0.6', lw=0.8)
ax.set_xlim(-0.3, 2.0); ax.set_ylim(-11, 11)
ax.set_title(r'$\sin(y/x)=\frac{1}{2}$: a fan of lines through $O$, $x>0$ only', fontsize=11)
ax.set_xlabel('x'); ax.set_ylabel('y')

plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

**Where the wrong options come from.**

| | |
|---|---|
| **E, F** (waves) | Read the equation as $y = \tfrac12\sin(\dots)$ — treated $\sin$ as acting on $x$. But $\tfrac{y}{x}$ is the argument, so the solutions are *constants*, giving lines, not a wave. |
| **A, C** | Lines through the origin, but drawn on **both** sides ($x<0$ too) — the restriction $-3\pi x \le y \le 3\pi x$ forces $x>0$, so the left half must be blank. |
| **D** | Too few lines, or only positive gradients — missed the two negative-gradient lines that still fit inside the wedge. |
:::

## Question 4

::: {.question}
The equation
$$\cos^2\!\left(4^{\sin\theta} \times 30^\circ\right) = \frac14$$
has exactly **two** solutions in the range $0^\circ \le \theta \le x^\circ$. What is the range of all
possible values of $x$?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $30 \le x < 150$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **B** $60 \le x < 180$ &nbsp;&nbsp;
**C** $60 \le x < 390$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **D** $90 \le x < 150$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **E** $90 \le x < 390$
:::

This is the hardest kind of graph question because the graph is buried under two layers — an exponential
inside a cosine. Peel it: [solve the outside first, then work inward]{.hl}. $\cos^2(\text{angle}) =
\tfrac14$ means $\cos(\text{angle}) = \pm\tfrac12$, which pins the angle to a short list; each value of
the angle then forces $4^{\sin\theta}$, and hence $\sin\theta$, and hence $\theta$. Once you have the
solution list $\theta = 30^\circ,\,90^\circ,\,150^\circ$, the final part is pure graph-reading:
[the letter $x$ is a moving right-hand endpoint, and you slide it until it has swept up exactly two
solutions]{.hl}.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(Set C/D Q19)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — solve by drawing; count where a curve meets a horizontal line, and read the counting condition
:::


**Peel the outer layer.** $\cos^2(\alpha) = \tfrac14 \Rightarrow \cos\alpha = \pm\tfrac12$, so the angle
$\alpha = 4^{\sin\theta}\times 30^\circ$ must be one of $60^\circ, 120^\circ, 240^\circ, \dots$

**Work inward.** On $0^\circ \le \theta \le 180^\circ$ we have $\sin\theta \in [0,1]$, so
$4^{\sin\theta} \in [1,4]$ and the angle $\alpha = 30\cdot 4^{\sin\theta}$ lives in $[30^\circ,
120^\circ]$. Only two target values fall in that band:

- $\alpha = 60^\circ \Rightarrow 4^{\sin\theta} = 2 \Rightarrow \sin\theta = \tfrac12 \Rightarrow
  \theta = 30^\circ \text{ or } 150^\circ.$
- $\alpha = 120^\circ \Rightarrow 4^{\sin\theta} = 4 \Rightarrow \sin\theta = 1 \Rightarrow
  \theta = 90^\circ.$

So there are exactly three solutions in $[0^\circ,180^\circ]$: [$\theta = 30^\circ,\,90^\circ,\,
150^\circ$]{.hl}.

**Slide the endpoint.** Reading left to right, the solutions arrive at $30$, then $90$, then $150$. The
window $[0, x]$ contains **exactly two** of them once it has passed $90$ but not yet reached $150$:
$$90 \le x < 150,$$
which is **option D**. (At $x=90$ the second solution is just included; at $x=150$ the third arrives and
you would have three.) $\blacksquare$

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "y = cos²(30·4^{sinθ}) against θ on [0,180]. It meets the line y=¼ at θ=30, 90, 150. A right-hand endpoint x has exactly two solutions to its left when 90 ≤ x < 150."
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

CURVE = '#1f77b4'; LEVEL = '#d62728'; HIT = '#2ca02c'

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.6, 4.4))

theta = np.linspace(0, 180, 800)
s = np.sin(np.deg2rad(theta))
alpha = 30*4.0**s                     # degrees
y = np.cos(np.deg2rad(alpha))**2
ax.plot(theta, y, color=CURVE, lw=2, label=r'$y=\cos^2(30\cdot 4^{\sin\theta})$')
ax.axhline(0.25, color=LEVEL, lw=1.3, ls='--', label=r'$y=\frac{1}{4}$')

for t in (30, 90, 150):
    ax.plot(t, 0.25, 'o', color=HIT)
    ax.annotate(fr'$\theta={t}$', (t, 0.25), (t-6, 0.33), fontsize=10, color=HIT)

# shade the winning window 90 <= x < 150
ax.axvspan(90, 150, color=HIT, alpha=0.12)
ax.text(120, 0.9, r'$90\leq x<150$', color=HIT, fontsize=11, ha='center')

ax.set_xlim(0, 180); ax.set_ylim(0, 1.02)
ax.set_xlabel(r'$\theta$ (degrees)'); ax.set_ylabel('y')
ax.set_xticks([0, 30, 60, 90, 120, 150, 180])
ax.legend(loc='lower left', fontsize=9)
ax.set_title('Three crossings; slide x to catch exactly two', fontsize=11)

plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

**Where the wrong options come from.**

| | |
|---|---|
| **A** $30 \le x < 150$ | Counted from the *first* solution — but at $x=30$ there is only **one** solution, not two. Off by one crossing. |
| **E** $90 \le x < 390$ | Right lower end, but let $\theta$ run past $180^\circ$ looking for more solutions. Beyond $180^\circ$, $\sin\theta<0$ so $4^{\sin\theta}<1$ and $\alpha<30^\circ$ — the target angles are never reached again in range. |
| **B, C** | Started the angle list at the wrong place (e.g. took $\cos\alpha=\tfrac12$ only, missing $-\tfrac12$), shifting every solution. |
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## The four moves, in one place

Every graph question on the TMUA is one of these. Name the move before you start:

1. **Read and feed** (Q1) — the graph is given; substitute $w=f(x)$ and read its range off the picture,
   then it is an ordinary interval problem.
2. **Decode the symmetry** (Q2) — "is it odd or even?" decides whether an integral doubles or cancels.
   $f(\lvert x\rvert)$ is always even.
3. **Constant ⇒ line** (Q3) — if solving forces $\tfrac{y}{x}$ (or any ratio) to equal constants, the
   graph is straight lines through the origin, never a curve.
4. **Draw and count** (Q4) — for "how many solutions", draw one curve and one line and count crossings;
   a moving endpoint is just a vertical line you slide.
:::

:::
